Audit a technical document and its accompanying test file. You have no prior context on either; form your own judgement from the artefacts and the codebase.

READ IN FULL:
1. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Desktop/TSD-SFCC-681-mrt-application-topology.md` — a Technical Solution Design (TSD) for a Salesforce Commerce Cloud PWA Kit project. It recommends a deployment topology for the storefront's server-side layer.
2. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts` — the test file the TSD cites as its evidence.
3. `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/TSD-PLAYBOOK-TIM-LAVELLE.md` — documented standards of the architect who must approve this TSD. The document is written to be approved by him.

The codebase is at `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa`. Project rules are in `AGENTS.md` and `.claude/rules/`. Companion docs are in `.docs/`.

Your task: determine whether this TSD is fit to submit for approval, and whether the test file genuinely supports what the TSD claims of it.

Check at minimum:
- **Factual accuracy.** Verify every checkable claim the TSD makes about the codebase against the actual code: file paths, function names, counts (of tests, files, integrations, environments, storefronts, proxies), arithmetic, and any claim about what code currently does or does not do. Run the test suite yourself.
- **Sourcing.** Does every factual claim trace to something a reviewer could check? Are cited sections/documents real and do they say what is attributed to them?
- **Internal consistency.** Does any part of the document contradict any other part? Do cross-references resolve? Are numbers consistent throughout?
- **Test integrity.** Does each test assert what its name and the TSD's description claim? Is any test redundant, misleading, or testing something other than what it is cited for? Are there ordering dependencies or hidden coupling? Run tests individually as well as together.
- **The playbook.** Work through its pre-submission checklist and its "patterns that reliably trigger a comment" table, and judge the TSD against each.
- **Anything else** that would cause a problem at review, or that is simply wrong.

Report findings ordered by severity, each with file:line and a suggested fix. Also state clearly what you checked and found to be **sound** — an accurate picture matters more than a long list, so do not manufacture findings to seem thorough, and do not soften genuine ones to seem agreeable. If the document is close to ready, say so; if it is not, say that plainly.

Problem Statement 26 27 ### 1.1 Context 28 29 The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all 30 server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to 31 integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token 32 validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, 33 SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme 34 (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. Integration build-out begins in the 35 coming sprints. 36 37 ### 1.2 Problem 38 39 How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, 40 has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not 41 a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology 42 determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive 43 to change once integration code exists across many systems. 44 45 Compounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's 46 `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not 47 starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and 48 response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and 49 three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. Seven per-origin connection pools 50 were written to address part of this (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported 51 nowhere and attached to no request. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the 52 in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection. 53 54 ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved 55 56 - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed 57 position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever 58 writes the first proxy. 59 - The missing error handling persists and compounds. It was found by chance in one of the only three 60 server-side integration touchpoints that exist today, and nothing in the codebase, review process, 61 or CI prevents the same pattern recurring as the remaining systems are built. 62 - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback 63 that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. 64 - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking 65 divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. 66 67 ### 1.4 Success Criteria 68 69 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how 70 integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 71 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, 72 with any inaccuracies in existing documentation identified and raised for correction (§7). 73 3. The present failure behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than 74 asserted. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 75 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket. 76 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without 77 re-opening the question. 78 79 --- 80 81 ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions 82 83 ### 2.1 Constraints 84 85 | Constraint | Detail | 86 | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 87 | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. *(Source: MRT Overview, opening constraint statement.)* | 88 | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. *(Source: MRT Overview, Bundles.)* | 89 | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. *(Source: MRT Overview, Projects and Organizations.)* Seven environments are in use: the six deployment tiers plus one ad-hoc test environment *(verified in Runtime Admin, 12 Aug 2026)*. | 90 | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** *(Source: MRT Overview, App Server and Rendering constraints.)* | 91 | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. *(Source: `.docs/prd/regional.md`; `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5 Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture.)* | 92 | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts share a **single first-party origin** (AU at the root, the other seven path-prefixed); the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. *(Sources: `architecture.md` §Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope; MRT Overview, Environments constraints.)* | 93 | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual *(Source: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §9 Performance Strategy; summarised in `.docs/architecture.md` > Pre-Build Decisions #3.)* Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | 94 | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | 95 | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | 96 97 ### 2.2 Assumptions 98 99 | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | 100 | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 101 | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and the number of integration modules the single application carries. | 102 | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | 103 104 --- 105 106 ## 3. Options Analysis 107 108 ### 3.1 Options Summary 109 110 | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | 111 | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | 112 | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing deploy pipeline (one workflow per tier: dev, test, sit, uat, stg, prod), version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound operation in any integration blocks every other concurrent request on that process (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | 113 | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | 114 115 ### 3.2 Option Detail 116 117 #### Option A: Single MRT application 118 119 One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All 120 integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single 121 Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by 122 construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one 123 hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its 124 weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than 125 infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). 126 127 #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* 128 129 The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as 130 its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and 131 credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses 132 precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised 133 specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. 134 135 It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or 136 budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications 137 created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a 138 general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as 139 an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent 140 directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own 141 B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable 142 Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for 143 backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an 144 externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in 145 Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment 146 defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a 147 storefront. 148 149 MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or 150 domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. 151 Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently 152 count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every 153 cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and 154 the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight 155 storefronts depend on. 156 157 The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and 158 the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. 159 160 --- 161 162 ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale 163 164 ### 4.1 Recommended Option 165 166 **Option A: Single MRT application, with per-integration safeguards in the server-side layer.** 167 168 ### 4.2 Rationale 169 170 Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off 171 between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an 172 integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A 173 is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost 174 because it is the current state. 175 176 The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of 177 the status quo, because the status quo includes gaps that are real and demonstrated: integration 178 modules do not consistently catch their own failures, three route handlers leave work unobserved, and 179 no upstream call carries a timeout short enough to fail before MRT's own execution ceiling does. 180 Option A is therefore recommended **with safeguards**: one bundle, but with each integration confined to its own module, 181 given its own connection pool with an independent connection cap and timeout budget, wrapped in its 182 own error boundary, and with every route registration observing the promise it starts. These are 183 specified in §5. Adopting Option A without them would settle the topology question while leaving the 184 isolation gap open, which is the state this document exists to close. 185 186 ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted 187 188 - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do 189 not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any 190 integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or 191 configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by 192 infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. 193 - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of 194 deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every 195 integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. 196 - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat 197 environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: anyone 198 who needs deploy or variable access for one integration necessarily has it for all of them. The 199 platform provides no way to scope either within a single project. Accepted; revisit if the team 200 composition changes such that per-integration scoping becomes necessary. 201 - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the 202 module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. 203 204 --- 205 206 ## 5. Technical Implementation 207 208 > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is 209 > deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own 210 > ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the 211 > gaps in §1.2 undefined. **Every file listed below is Tier 1 in some form**, so the implementing 212 > ticket must secure approval before starting: `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `config/default.js` are 213 > absolute Tier 1 under Hard Rule #4 (§2.1); the four modules under `overrides/app/ssr/` are Tier 1 214 > Runtime & Integration Config, owned by Integration / SI Partner; and `.claude/rules/` is Tier 1 215 > Governance, requiring both squad leads and the Integration lead. 216 217 ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 218 219 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in 220 `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 221 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under 222 `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 223 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its 224 own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is 225 capped independently of every other integration. 226 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a 227 slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution 228 ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 229 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 230 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it 231 at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a 232 dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful 233 degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 234 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the **entire** promise 235 chain it starts, not merely its final call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved 236 floating promise. Three routes do not do this today (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud 237 failure, or an invalid SLAS callback token, currently produces no response at all rather than an 238 error response. 239 240 ### 5.2 Component / API Changes 241 242 | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | 243 | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | 244 | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Confirm pool definitions against real hostnames; resolve the three placeholder origins (`sfccPaymentsPool`, `booxiPool`, and `mulesoftPool`, whose env-var fallback is also a placeholder). Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. | Modified | 245 | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` inside `jwksCaching()`, currently a bare global-dispatcher call. | Modified | 246 | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the `fetch` inside `paymentMetadataHandler()`. | Modified | 247 | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on both `fetch` calls inside `sendMarketingCloudEmail()` (token exchange, then email send). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | 248 | `overrides/app/ssr.js` **(absolute Tier 1)** | Attach a `.catch()` to the **whole promise chain** in the passwordless-login and reset-password callback routes, not only to `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)`. `validateSlasCallbackToken` throws on an invalid or expired token (`slasTokens.ts:33,51`) and its chain is equally unobserved, so catching the inner call alone leaves the auth path failing silently. Also observe the `jwksCaching(...)` call in the JWKS route. Three route registrations currently leave a promise unobserved. | Modified | 249 | `config/default.js` **(Tier 1)** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | 250 | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | 251 | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | 252 253 ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces 254 255 The contract every integration module must satisfy: 256 257 ```ts 258 // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. 259 import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; 260 261 // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. 262 const response = await fetch(url, { 263 method: 'POST', 264 headers: { /* ... */ }, 265 body: JSON.stringify(payload), 266 dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts 267 }); 268 269 // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. 270 type IntegrationResult = 271 | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } 272 | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; 273 274 // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. 275 app.post(path, (req, res) => { 276 void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { 277 // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered 278 }); 279 }); 280 ``` 281 282 Pool boundaries, origins and connection caps are defined in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 and are 283 deliberately not restated here, to avoid two copies drifting apart. Those caps are derived from 284 expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass 285 described in §9.3 of that document. 286 287 **What the pools add.** Node's `fetch` already creates a separate connection pool per upstream origin 288 by default: `undici`'s `Agent` maintains one `Pool` per origin 289 (`node_modules/undici/lib/dispatcher/agent.js`). A slow integration therefore does not starve an 290 unrelated one, and that is not what explicit pools are for. What the default does **not** provide is 291 a bound on how many connections a single origin may open, or a response timeout short enough to fail 292 before MRT's execution ceiling. Explicit pools add exactly those two things: a **bound** per origin, 293 so one integration under load cannot consume unbounded sockets or overwhelm its upstream, and a 294 **timeout** that lets the integration fail cleanly and return an error rather than the platform 295 terminating the whole request. 296 297 ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases 298 299 | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | 300 | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | 301 | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | 302 | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, so the integration returns an explicit error instead of the whole request being terminated by the platform. | Error | 303 | An integration issues a burst of upstream calls | Its own pool caps the concurrent connections, so the burst queues within that integration rather than opening unbounded sockets and pressuring process file descriptors or the upstream itself. | Edge case | 304 | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | 305 | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | 306 | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation, per the constraint in §2.1. | Edge case | 307 | SLAS callback validation (`jose` fetches the JWKS itself, `slasTokens.ts:38`) | Also outside this pattern: `jose` takes no `dispatcher`. It is not unprotected, however: it applies its own 5s `timeoutDuration` and caches keys for 30s to 10 minutes, so it is low-frequency and already bounded. Left as-is; revisit only if its own defaults prove unsuitable. | Edge case | 308 309 ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes 310 311 No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration 312 adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** 313 `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. 314 315 --- 316 317 ## 6. Testing & Validation 318 319 ### 6.1 Test Coverage 320 321 Mapping to §1.4 criterion 3. Three tests exist and pass today 322 (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`). The table below also specifies two further rows that are 323 deliberately not yet written, and says why. 324 325 | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | 326 | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 327 | Unit / Integration | Asymmetric error handling across the real modules: `sendMagicLinkEmail` and `paymentMetadataHandler` run concurrently against the same upstream failure. | Currently: `sendMagicLinkEmail` rejects out of its module uncaught, while `paymentMetadataHandler` catches its own failure and still responds. After §5: both catch at their own boundary and return an explicit outcome. | 328 | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | 329 | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | 330 | Integration | Once §5 is implemented: that each pool's connection cap is actually enforced under load, and that its timeout fires before MRT's execution ceiling. Note this deliberately does **not** test cross-origin isolation, which §5.3 shows already holds by default. | Concurrency against one origin stays at or below its configured cap; a hung upstream fails through the pool's own timeout and returns an error, rather than running out MRT's 20s/16s ceiling. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | 331 | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | 332 333 Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are 334 already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is 335 already gated in CI. 336 337 ### 6.2 Regression Risk 338 339 The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 340 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to 341 existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and 342 Marketing Cloud email, all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would 343 surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The three tests above cover 344 the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap or timeout tuning, which is why the load-test row is 345 listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the 346 route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. One factor usefully 347 bounds the blast radius of both: a `dispatcher` is passed per call site, so only the four SSR `fetch` 348 calls listed in §5.2 change behaviour. Everything else, including all commerce traffic issued through 349 `commerce-sdk-react`, is untouched by definition. 350 351 --- 352 353 ## 7. 1	# TSD Playbook: Writing for Tim Lavelle's Approval
2	
3	A working reference distilled from Tim Lavelle's (Solution Architect) review comments on the Contentful Integration TSD (Confluence 346783750, SFCC-249) and related Jira tickets (SFCC-51, SFCC-96, SFCC-123, SFCC-249).
4	
5	Purpose: get a TSD to sign-off in fewer rounds by writing it the way he reviews it. Each principle below is paired with the actual comment it comes from, so the reasoning stays checkable rather than becoming folklore.
6	
7	**The one-line version:** Tim reviews for *trust* and *future maintenance cost*, not for completeness. A short document where every claim is traceable beats a thorough one where any claim is invented.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 1. Verify. Never pass through unreviewed AI output.
12	
13	> "Is this verified or a Claude assumption?"
14	> "I know this is Claude generated, but we should still be reviewing the output and be determining if Claude..."
15	
16	**Why it matters to him:** one invented claim makes every other claim suspect, and he has to re-verify the whole document himself. The cost isn't the single error, it's the loss of confidence in the artefact.
17	
18	**What to do:**
19	- Every factual claim traces to a source: a codebase path (ideally `file:line`), a Jira key, a Confluence page ID, or a named person's decision.
20	- Separate **built today** from **target architecture**. He caught exactly this: SSR-first fetch, GraphQL and the publish webhook were listed as current behaviour when none existed in code.
21	- Never state proposed design as if implemented. If it's proposed, the document says "proposed, not yet implemented."
22	- He is not anti-AI. On SFCC-96 he asked to "work with Claude around defining Accessibility requirements." He objects to *unreviewed* output, not to the tool.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 2. One problem per TSD.
27	
28	> "MRT-app architecture is out of scope here; covered by a separate TSD (SFCC-237)."
29	> "This would be dependent on the MRT node application TSD we still need to look at."
30	
31	**Why it matters to him:** a TSD carrying several unrelated problems can never be signed off, because it's blocked on every one of those decisions at once. Scope discipline is what makes approval possible.
32	
33	**What to do:**
34	- State the single problem in the Problem Statement and hold to it.
35	- Anything adjacent gets linked out to its own TSD or raised as a ticket, not absorbed.
36	- If a section depends on an undecided TSD, say so and defer it rather than guessing.
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 3. Link, don't replicate. This is the drift-risk rule.
41	
42	> "This is why I would prefer not to put specifics like these in the TSD and it can drift quickly and we need to update multiple pages."
43	> "Is this the same approach as documented in the parent page and if so, let's not replicate as could introduce drift. If it is the same, we can remove this table and reference the parent."
44	
45	**Why it matters to him:** duplicated content is a maintenance liability. When the underlying fact changes, someone has to find and update every copy, and in practice they won't. His concern is the future cost, not present accuracy.
46	
47	**What to do:**
48	- If it already exists in a parent page, runbook, or Jira card, link it. Do not restate it.
49	- Volatile specifics (field sets, content-model catalogues, counts) belong in the ticket or a dedicated requirements page, not in the TSD body.
50	- Before adding any table, ask: does this exist elsewhere? If yes, reference it.
51	- He raised this same objection at least four separate times on one document. It is his most repeated review theme.
52	
53	---
54	
55	## 4. Real work, tested. Paper designs get pushback.
56	
57	> "This is where I would love to see some real work done and tested."
58	> "the team needs to do a **Technical Solution Design** and POC on how we integrate..." (SFCC-51)
59	
60	**Why it matters to him:** a design that has never been exercised is an assumption with formatting. He wants the TSD paired with something demonstrated.
61	
62	**What to do:**
63	- Pair the TSD with a POC or spike where feasible, and reference it.
64	- Where something is unproven, label it plainly rather than writing around it.
65	- Distinguish "proven in this codebase" from "designed on paper" from "vendor-documented capability."
66	
67	---
68	
69	## 5. Name the owner and the next action.
70	
71	> "my concern is who is responsible for this scope?"
72	> "I like this, but where are we logging this and how?"
73	> "I agree with this, but similar to the Log comment above, what are we doing with this incident?"
74	
75	**Why it matters to him:** an open item with no owner never closes. A described behaviour with no operational answer isn't implementable.
76	
77	**What to do:**
78	- Every open item carries an Owner and a next action.
79	- Every operational statement answers where, how, and who.
80	- "Pending X, owned by Y" is an acceptable answer. Silence is not.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## 6. Check the current state of the world before you write.
85	
86	> "We've already boostrapped all the Contentful Environments and aliases, we won't be using different Spaces for this project any longer."
87	> "This row isn't needed, they are on the enterprise plan"
88	> "This is now redundant as we have a process for creating our local env files."
89	> "let's get one of the developers to review the current PWA Kit Navigation to see what of these functionalities it already has" (SFCC-96)
90	
91	**Why it matters to him:** documenting a constraint that reality has already resolved burns his review cycle on corrections rather than substance. Several rows were removed purely because the world had moved on.
92	
93	**What to do:**
94	- Before writing constraints, options, or risks: confirm current state with the SA and check the codebase.
95	- Ask "is this still true?" rather than inferring from an older document.
96	- Check what the platform already provides before designing something new.
97	
98	---
99	
100	## 7. No vague language, no unexplained numbers.
101	
102	> "What do we mean by this?"
103	> "What is this 10th. locale this section is assuming?"
104	
105	**Why it matters to him:** vagueness transfers the interpretive burden onto the reviewer. If he has to guess what a sentence means, he'll ask instead, and that's a round trip.
106	
107	**What to do:**
108	- No undefined jargon, no figures that appear without derivation.
109	- State the specific mechanism, not the category of mechanism.
110	- If something is genuinely undecided, write it as explicitly undecided with the options named. That reads as rigour, not as a gap.
111	
112	---
113	
114	## 8. Don't over-engineer distinctions.
115	
116	> "I'm not sure we need to seperate these and the components we build will most of the time being used in an experience builder."
117	
118	**Why it matters to him:** a rule that doesn't change any outcome is cognitive load without payoff.
119	
120	**What to do:**
121	- Only introduce a rule, split, or category if you can point to a concrete case where it changes the decision.
122	- Lead with that case, not with the abstraction.
123	
124	---
125	
126	## 9. Route content to the right artefact.
127	
128	> "Let's document these in the Jira cards respectively"
129	> "this feels a bit repetitive from some of the above sections, can we review and move to the appropriate sections?"
130	> "We should consider component requirement pages where we capture these content models and development requirements."
131	
132	**Why it matters to him:** each artefact has a job. Content in the wrong one is both harder to find and harder to keep current.
133	
134	| Content | Belongs in |
135	| --- | --- |
136	| The decision, the options weighed, and why | TSD |
137	| Buildable requirement and acceptance criteria | Jira card |
138	| Operational steps, environment setup, credentials | Runbook |
139	| Content models, field sets, component specifics | Requirements page or the ticket |
140	| Cross-cutting architecture | Its own TSD, linked |
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 10. Bring the right people in before review, not as a gap at review.
145	
146	> "Please make sure we involve and/or get input from Jesse C. Pagaduan on this item"
147	> "need to run the authoring approach by Emma and Dani"
148	> "we should be asking Emma/IT if they are going to procure NewRelic"
149	
150	**Why it matters to him:** he doesn't want to discover at sign-off that a specialist was never consulted. That's a round trip he can't shortcut.
151	
152	**Known routing on this project:** QA to Jesse C. Pagaduan. Content authoring to Emma Kirwan and Dani Rivett. MRT architecture to Gideon. Procurement and IT to Emma. Requirements and AC to Jasmijn Tsang (BA Lead). Design specs to the design team via Figma.
153	
154	---
155	
156	## 11. Unknowns become explicit to-dos, not silent assumptions.
157	
158	> "we need to do a spike to ensure we can capture the # in the SFCC PLP and inject this item into it and test how it affects item counts and pagination. Not needed now, but capturing as a to do."
159	
160	**Why it matters to him:** he is comfortable with unknowns. He is not comfortable with unknowns dressed up as decisions. A tracked gap is safe; a confident guess is a liability.
161	
162	**What to do:**
163	- Write "undecided, pending X, owner Y" rather than picking a plausible answer.
164	- Raise the spike or ticket, and reference it.
165	- An honest gap is more approvable than a confident guess. This is the single highest-leverage habit in this list.
166	
167	---
168	
169	## Pre-submission checklist
170	
171	Run this before asking for his review.
172	
173	**Trust**
174	- [ ] Every factual claim has a traceable source
175	- [ ] Current state and target state are visibly separated
176	- [ ] Nothing proposed is written as if implemented
177	- [ ] Claims about the codebase were checked against the actual working branch
178	
179	**Scope**
180	- [ ] One problem, stated plainly
181	- [ ] Adjacent problems linked out, not absorbed
182	- [ ] Dependencies on other TSDs named rather than assumed
183	
184	**Drift**
185	- [ ] No table or section duplicates a parent page
186	- [ ] Volatile specifics live in the ticket or requirements page, not here
187	- [ ] Cross-references point at a single source of truth
188	
189	**Accountability**
190	- [ ] Every open item has an owner and a next action
191	- [ ] Every operational claim answers where, how, who
192	- [ ] Affected specialists were consulted, and that's recorded
193	
194	**Language**
195	- [ ] No unexplained numbers or undefined jargon
196	- [ ] Undecided items explicitly labelled undecided
197	- [ ] No em dashes or en dashes (project writing convention)
198	
199	---
200	
201	## Patterns that reliably trigger a comment
202	
203	| Pattern | What he'll say |
204	| --- | --- |
205	| A confident claim with no source | "Is this verified or a Claude assumption?" |
206	| A table that also exists on a parent page | "let's not replicate as could introduce drift" |
207	| A number with no derivation | "What is this X this section is assuming?" |
208	| Target architecture written as current | (correction, with the code as counter-evidence) |
209	| An open item with no owner | "who is responsible for this scope?" |
210	| Behaviour described with no operational detail | "where are we logging this and how?" |
211	| A rule with no demonstrated need | "I'm not sure we need to separate these" |
212	| A design never exercised | "I would love to see some real work done and tested" |
213	| A constraint that reality already resolved | "This row isn't needed" / "This is now redundant" |
214	
215	---
216	
217	## Provenance
218	
219	Sources: inline review comments on Confluence 346783750 (versions up to v42), and Jira comments on SFCC-51, SFCC-96, SFCC-123, SFCC-249. Quotes are verbatim from those comments, including original typos.
220	
221	Distinction worth keeping: items 1 to 7 and 9 to 11 are directly evidenced by his own words. Item 8 reflects one comment (the Studio-versus-coded authoring path) that is still an open disagreement at time of writing, not a settled preference, so treat it as a tendency rather than a rule.
222	
223	Related: the "one TSD, one problem" principle also appears in the prescribed TSD template (Confluence 352419841).
